questions.q: What does `KafkaProducer.send(record)` do when it is called?

options.t: It blocks until every in-sync replica has stored the record
options.why: send() is asynchronous; waiting is what get() on the returned Future does.

options.t: It adds the record to a buffer and returns a Future at once
It writes the record to the local disk, then to the broker
options.why: The producer keeps pending records in memory, not on disk.

options.t: It opens a new connection to the leader for this one record
options.why: The producer reuses connections and batches records.

questions.explain: `send()` is asynchronous: it adds the record to a buffer of pending sends and returns a `Future<RecordMetadata>` immediately. Calling `get()` on it blocks until the request completes.

questions.q: A web service has 32 request threads that each send to Kafka. How should it use producers?

options.t: Create a new producer for every request and close it afterwards
options.why: Producers are expensive to create and are meant to be long-lived and shared.

options.t: One producer per thread, because KafkaProducer is not thread safe
options.why: KafkaProducer is thread safe; it's KafkaConsumer that isn't.

options.t: Share one producer instance across the threads
One producer per partition, chosen by each thread
options.why: One producer writes to every partition; partitioning is per record.

questions.explain: The producer is thread safe, and the Javadoc says sharing a single instance across threads will generally be faster than having multiple instances.

questions.q: Where do producer send callbacks run, and what follows from that?

options.t: In the producer's I/O thread, so slow ones delay other sends
In a new thread per callback, so they can block freely
options.why: Callbacks generally run in the single I/O thread, so blocking in them is harmful.

options.t: In the thread that called send(), after it returns
options.why: send() returns before the record is acknowledged; the callback runs later in the I/O thread.

options.t: On the broker, which runs them before it acknowledges the batch
options.why: Callbacks are client code and run in the client.

questions.explain: Callbacks generally execute in the producer's I/O thread and should be reasonably fast; otherwise they delay sending messages from other threads.

questions.q: Records A, B and C are sent, in that order, to the same partition with a callback each. In what order do the callbacks run?

options.t: In any order, depending on network timing
options.why: For one partition, the order is guaranteed.

options.t: C, B, A, newest first
options.why: There is no reverse ordering.

options.t: Only the last callback runs, for the whole batch
options.why: Each record's callback runs.

options.t: A, B, C: callbacks for one partition run in order

questions.explain: The Javadoc guarantees that callbacks for records sent to the same partition execute in order.

questions.q: A batch job sends 10 000 records with `send()` and then exits. Some records never arrive. What should it call before exiting?

options.t: send() again for every record, with acks=0
options.why: Resending doesn't make sure buffered records go out before exit.

options.t: flush() or close()
commitSync(), which forces the producer to send
options.why: commitSync() is a consumer method for offsets.

options.t: Nothing; send() already waited for each record
options.why: send() returns before the record is sent.

questions.explain: `flush()` makes buffered records immediately sendable and blocks until their requests complete; `close()` blocks until all previously sent requests complete.

questions.q: A shutdown hook calls `producer.close(Duration.ofSeconds(5))`, and some requests are still in flight after 5 seconds. What happens to them?

options.t: They are written to a local file and sent on the next start
options.why: The producer has no on-disk spool.

options.t: close() keeps waiting until they all complete
options.why: That is close() without a timeout.

options.t: They fail at once, and an open transaction is aborted
They are handed to another producer in the same process
options.why: Producers don't hand records to each other.

questions.explain: `close(Duration)` waits up to the timeout, then fails any unsent and unacknowledged records immediately, and aborts an ongoing transaction.

questions.q: In Kafka 4.3, what are the producer's defaults for `linger.ms` and `batch.size`?

options.t: linger.ms=0 and batch.size=16384
options.why: linger.ms changed from 0 to 5 in Kafka 4.0.

options.t: linger.ms=100 and batch.size=1048576
options.why: Neither is a default; 1 MiB is max.request.size.

options.t: linger.ms=10 and batch.size=32768
options.why: These are tuning choices some guides suggest, not the defaults.

options.t: linger.ms=5 and batch.size=16384

questions.explain: `linger.ms` defaults to 5 (it changed from 0 in Kafka 4.0) and `batch.size` to 16384 bytes (16 KiB).

questions.q: A producer sends small records at a high rate and the team wants more throughput. Which TWO changes are most likely to help?

options.t: Raise linger.ms a little so batches fill up more
Set batch.size=0
options.why: 0 disables batching, which lowers throughput.

options.t: Enable compression such as lz4 or zstd, which works better on bigger batches
Set acks=all and min.insync.replicas=3
options.why: These raise durability, not throughput.

options.t: Set max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=1
options.why: Fewer requests in flight reduces throughput.

questions.explain: Batching trades a little latency for throughput: a slightly longer linger fills bigger batches, and compression works on whole batches, so better batching gives better compression.

questions.q: Brokers become slow and the producer's buffer fills up. What happens to the next `send()` call with default settings?

options.t: It throws BufferExhaustedException at once
options.why: send() first blocks, up to max.block.ms.

options.t: It drops the oldest buffered record to make room
options.why: The producer never drops buffered records to make room.

options.t: It blocks for up to max.block.ms (60 s), then fails if no space frees up
It doubles buffer.memory automatically
options.why: buffer.memory is fixed by configuration.

questions.explain: `buffer.memory` (32 MiB) bounds records waiting to be sent. When it is full, `send()` blocks for up to `max.block.ms` (60 000 ms) and then fails.

questions.q: Which compression types can a Kafka producer use with `compression.type`?

options.t: none, gzip, snappy, lz4, zstd
zip, rar, gzip
options.why: zip and rar are not Kafka codecs.

options.t: Only gzip
options.why: Kafka supports several codecs.

options.t: none and deflate, chosen per record
options.why: Compression is per batch, and deflate is not one of the options.

questions.explain: `compression.type` takes `none` (the default), `gzip`, `snappy`, `lz4` or `zstd`, and compresses whole batches.

questions.q: A topic has `compression.type=producer` (the default). A producer sends zstd-compressed batches. What does the broker store, and who decompresses?

options.t: The broker decompresses and stores the records uncompressed
options.why: With the producer setting, the batch stays compressed in the log.

options.t: The broker recompresses everything with gzip
options.why: That would need compression.type=gzip on the topic.

options.t: zstd batches, decompressed only by the consumer
The consumer must use the same producer instance to decompress
options.why: Any consumer can decompress; the codec is recorded in the batch.

questions.explain: The topic's `producer` setting keeps the producer's codec. Compressed batches stay compressed in the log and are decompressed by the consumer (end-to-end batch compression).

questions.q: The Kafka documentation recommends controlling how long a producer keeps retrying a send with which setting?

options.t: retries, set to a small number such as 3
options.why: The docs prefer leaving retries unset and using delivery.timeout.ms.

options.t: request.timeout.ms
options.why: That bounds one request, not all retries.

options.t: max.block.ms
options.why: That bounds how long send() itself may block.

options.t: delivery.timeout.ms

questions.explain: `retries` defaults to the maximum integer, and the docs prefer leaving it unset and using `delivery.timeout.ms` (default 2 minutes), which bounds waiting, the ack and retries together.

questions.q: Which statement about the producer's retry backoff in Kafka 4.3 is right?

options.t: It is fixed at retry.backoff.ms for every attempt
options.why: It grows exponentially up to retry.backoff.max.ms.

options.t: Exponential from 100 ms to 1 s, with ±20% jitter
It is chosen by the broker in each error response
options.why: The client computes the backoff.

options.t: There is no backoff; retries are immediate
options.why: Kafka backs off, with jitter.

questions.explain: The backoff starts at `retry.backoff.ms` and grows exponentially to `retry.backoff.max.ms`, with ±20% random jitter so clients don't retry in sync.

questions.q: A producer has `enable.idempotence=false`, `retries` above 0 and `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5`. What risk does this create?

options.t: None; ordering within a partition is always kept by the broker
options.why: Without idempotence, retries with several requests in flight can reorder.

options.t: Records may be written to the wrong partition
options.why: Partition choice is not affected by retries.

options.t: The producer will refuse to start
options.why: This is a valid, if risky, configuration.

options.t: A retried batch can land after a later one, reordering records

questions.explain: With idempotence off and more than one request in flight, retries can reorder records. Idempotence keeps order with up to 5 in flight, because the broker retains up to 5 batches per producer.

questions.q: A developer explicitly sets `enable.idempotence=true` and also `acks=1`. What happens?

options.t: The producer starts, and idempotence is silently turned off
options.why: Silent disabling happens only when idempotence was not explicitly enabled.

options.t: The producer starts with acks=all instead
options.why: The client doesn't rewrite the setting; it rejects it.

options.t: Creating the producer fails with a ConfigException
It works; idempotence doesn't depend on acks
options.why: Idempotence requires acks=all.

questions.explain: Idempotence requires `acks=all`, retries > 0 and at most 5 requests in flight. If it is explicitly enabled with conflicting settings, the producer throws `ConfigException`.

questions.q: A team needs records routed by a business rule that the key hash doesn't express (for example VIP customers to partition 0). What does Kafka provide for this?

options.t: Implement the Partitioner interface and set partitioner.class
Set partitioner.ignore.keys=true
options.why: That ignores keys entirely; it doesn't apply a business rule.

options.t: Use a topic per partition
options.why: That changes the data model instead of routing within a topic.

options.t: Ask the broker to route by value with a topic setting
options.why: Partitions are chosen by the producer, not the broker.

questions.explain: A custom partitioner implements `Partitioner` and is set with `partitioner.class`. (The application can also set the partition on each record.)

questions.q: Which TWO statements about the producer's built-in partitioning in Kafka 4.3 are right?

options.t: A keyed record goes to the partition chosen by hashing its key
DefaultPartitioner must be set explicitly to get key hashing
options.why: DefaultPartitioner was removed in 4.0; the built-in logic applies when partitioner.class is null.

options.t: With adaptive partitioning (on by default), the producer sends more to partitions on faster brokers
Keyless records always go to partition 0
options.why: Keyless records go to a sticky partition that changes.

options.t: partitioner.ignore.keys defaults to true
options.why: It defaults to false.

questions.explain: With `partitioner.class` unset, a key is hashed to choose the partition, and keyless records use a sticky partition. `partitioner.adaptive.partitioning.enable` (default true) favours faster brokers.

questions.q: A send callback fires with a non-null exception. What does the RecordMetadata argument contain?

options.t: The partition and offset the record would have had
options.why: There is no offset on failure: it is -1.

options.t: null
options.why: The callback always gets a metadata object; on failure its values are -1.

options.t: -1 in every field, even when a partition had been chosen
options.why: The 4.3 source keeps the chosen topic-partition; the partition is -1 only if none could be chosen.

options.t: The chosen topic-partition, if any, with -1 for the offset

questions.explain: On failure the offset and the other values are -1. The Javadoc adds that the partition is -1 only if it cannot be chosen, and the Kafka 4.3 source builds the failure metadata with the chosen topic-partition. On success the metadata holds the record's partition and offset.

questions.q: Which TWO of these errors in a producer callback are retriable, meaning a retry may succeed?

options.t: NotEnoughReplicasException
RecordTooLargeException
options.why: A record that is too large will be too large on every attempt.

options.t: AuthorizationException
options.why: Missing permissions don't fix themselves by retrying.

options.t: TimeoutException
InvalidTopicException
options.why: An invalid topic name stays invalid.

questions.explain: The Callback Javadoc lists `NotEnoughReplicasException` and `TimeoutException` among retriable (transient) errors, and `RecordTooLargeException`, `AuthorizationException` and `InvalidTopicException` among non-retriable ones.

questions.q: An application's callback sees a `NotEnoughReplicasException` after the producer has been running for two minutes during a broker outage. Why did the producer not retry it away?

options.t: It retried until delivery.timeout.ms ran out
NotEnoughReplicasException is never retried by the producer
options.why: It is a retriable exception; the producer retries it.

options.t: Retries are off by default
options.why: retries defaults to the maximum integer.

options.t: The broker told the producer not to retry
options.why: Retry is a client decision for retriable errors.

questions.explain: The producer retries retriable errors itself, bounded by `delivery.timeout.ms` (2 minutes by default). The application sees a retriable error only when retrying has run out of time.

questions.q: `send()` is called with a value the configured serializer can't handle. How is the error delivered?

options.t: Through the callback, after retries
options.why: Serialization happens in send() itself, so the error is thrown there.

options.t: send() throws SerializationException directly
The broker rejects the batch with CorruptRecordException
options.why: The record never reaches the broker.

options.t: It is silently dropped
options.why: The Javadoc lists SerializationException as thrown by send().

questions.explain: The `send()` Javadoc lists `SerializationException`, thrown when the key or value is not valid for the configured serializers.
